content: 1. Depression, endometriosis, diabetes mellitus (DM), hypertension (HTN), changes in bone mineral density, renal or hepatic impairment, bone metabolic disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) are conditions that may require careful monitoring when using certain therapies. Additionally, conditions exacerbated by fluid retention, such as migraines, asthma, and epilepsy, should be considered. 2. Women with a history of depression should be closely monitored, and therapy should be discontinued if depression recurs to a severe degree. 3. Women with a history of hypertension, hypertension-related diseases, or renal disease should be encouraged to use alternative methods of contraception. 4. Therapy should be discontinued if the following conditions develop: jaundice, visual problems (which may cause contact lens intolerance), any signs of venous thromboembolism (VTE), migraines with unusual severity, significant increases in blood pressure, severe depression, or an increased risk of thromboembolic complications following surgery. 5. In women with hereditary angioedema, exogenous estrogens may induce or exacerbate symptoms of angioedema. 6. Therapy should be discontinued four weeks prior to major surgery or prolonged immobilization. 7. Patients on warfarin or oral anticoagulants may require an increase in anticoagulant dosage. 8. There is an increased risk of cervical cancer with oral contraceptive pill (OCP) use; however, human papillomavirus (HPV) remains the primary risk factor for this cancer. Evidence suggests that long-term use of OCPs (five or more years) may be associated with an increased risk. 9. There is an increased risk of liver cancer with OCP use, and the risk increases with longer durations of use. 10. The risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) is highest during the first year of OCP use and when a combination oral contraceptive is started or restarted after a break of four weeks or more. 11. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) guidelines recommend waiting at least three weeks following vaginal birth or six weeks after cesarean section before initiating combined hormonal contraceptives to decrease the risk of VTE. Women with additional risk factors for VTE (besides being postpartum) should not use combined hormonal contraceptives. 12. Hormonal therapy should be discontinued prior to starting therapy with the combination drug regimen ombitasvir/paritaprevir/ritonavir, with or without dasabuvir. Hormonal therapy may be restarted approximately two weeks following the completion of treatment with the combination drug regimen. 13. Chloasma may occur with OCP use, especially in women with a history of chloasma gravidarum. Women with a history of chloasma should be advised to avoid exposure to sunlight or ultraviolet radiation while on therapy. 14. Extensive epidemiological studies have shown no increased risk of birth defects in women who have used OCPs prior to pregnancy. Studies also do not suggest a teratogenic effect, particularly concerning cardiac anomalies and limb reduction defects, when OCPs are inadvertently taken during early pregnancy. 15. The administration of OCPs to induce withdrawal bleeding should not be used as a test for pregnancy. OCPs should not be used during pregnancy to treat threatened or habitual abortion. 16. For any patient who has missed two consecutive periods, pregnancy should be ruled out before continuing OCP use. If the patient has not adhered to the prescribed schedule, the possibility of pregnancy should be considered at the time of the first missed period. OCP use should be discontinued if pregnancy is confirmed. 17. Small amounts of OCP steroids have been identified in the milk of nursing mothers, and a few adverse effects on the child have been reported, including jaundice and breast enlargement. Additionally, OCPs given in the postpartum period may interfere with lactation by decreasing the quantity and quality of breast milk. If possible, nursing mothers should be advised not to use OCPs and to use other forms of contraception until they have completely weaned their child. 18. When initially starting OCPs, an additional contraceptive method should be used during the first consecutive seven days of administration. 19. OCPs should be started on the first day of the menstrual cycle or on the Sunday immediately following the onset of menses.
